items.title: No Surprises Act payment dispute process booms to $22.4 billion cost in 4 years: study - Medical Economics
items.reason: This item reports on the financial impact and operational scale of the No Surprises Act's Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process, which is a core implementation mechanism directly affecting revenue-cycle operations and payment dispute handling.
items.summary: A new study found that the No Surprises Act's Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) payment dispute process has accumulated $22.4 billion in costs over a four-year period. The IDR process, established under the federal No Surprises Act to resolve out-of-network payment disputes between providers and insurers, has grown substantially in volume and associated administrative expenses. This development directly impacts healthcare revenue-cycle teams by demonstrating the significant financial burden of dispute resolution compliance and the scale of payment disagreements occurring under the law's balance-billing protections.

items.title: AG Brown sues United Healthcare, Optum for defrauding Maryland Medicaid Program - WBFF
items.reason: This is a state attorney-general lawsuit against UnitedHealthcare and its parent Optum alleging fraud against a Medicaid program, which directly matches the payer litigation and enforcement category in the topic definition.
items.summary: Maryland Attorney General Brown filed a lawsuit against UnitedHealthcare and Optum alleging fraud against the Maryland Medicaid program. The suit represents enforcement action by a state attorney general against a major payer, with implications for how UnitedHealthcare manages Medicaid claims processing and member eligibility determinations. Revenue-cycle teams should monitor this case for potential precedent on payer fraud liability, claims-handling practices, and possible penalties or compliance requirements that could affect reimbursement workflows and audit obligations.

items.title: Humana-owned Villages Health agrees to $542M settlement for overbilling Medicare
items.reason: This item reports a major settlement involving a Humana-owned entity (payer-adjacent provider network) for alleged Medicare Advantage billing fraud, which directly falls under CMS/Medicare Advantage sanctions and enforcement actions against payer organizations.
items.summary: Humana-owned Villages Health has agreed to a $542 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Justice for overbilling Medicare Advantage from 2020 to 2024 by manufacturing fake diagnosis codes for its patient population. The settlement represents a significant CMS enforcement action against a major payer subsidiary and signals increased regulatory scrutiny of diagnosis coding practices in MA plans. Revenue-cycle teams should note heightened audit risks around diagnosis coding accuracy and the potential for retroactive claim denials or rate adjustments, particularly in MA programs where Humana or other major payers operate affiliated provider networks.

This litigation affects Cigna's claims administration practices and carries financial exposure that healthcare revenue-cycle teams monitor for broader payer enforcement trends and claims-denial patterns.

items.title: UnitedHealth Shareholder Lawsuit: Company Rushed Change Integration to Make It Irreversible, Killed Medicare Audit - HEALTH CARE un-covered
items.reason: This item reports a shareholder lawsuit against UnitedHealth involving allegations of mismanagement related to a business integration and Medicare audit termination, which falls within payer litigation and enforcement actions involving a major national health insurer.
items.summary: A shareholder lawsuit has been filed against UnitedHealth alleging the company rushed an integration process to make it irreversible and terminated a Medicare audit. The suit claims UnitedHealth made strategic decisions regarding a business combination integration and subsequently killed an internal Medicare audit, suggesting potential fiduciary concerns. This litigation against a major national payer involves claims of mismanagement that could relate to operational and compliance failures. The case is relevant to revenue-cycle teams as it may implicate broader payer governance and audit practices affecting claims processing and compliance obligations.
